slides.title: Hair is hard
slides.speech: Peekaboo and Illusions steer pixels the model already makes. Transparency it can't make at all, it only outputs RGB, and Peekaboo's blobby masks showed that gap. This is an alpha matte: white is the object, black is background, gray strands are partly see-through. Matting datasets are made by hand, so they stop at a few hundred objects; the largest general-purpose one has 726. Segmentation sets like COCO are huge, but their edges are hard outlines. So here the handle is data: can a frozen RGB model build a big alpha dataset for us?

slides.title: The trick

elements.text: B = the screen color, known at every pixel

slides.speech: The trick is embarrassingly simple: ask for the object on a solid green screen, then chroma key it like Hollywood. Every pixel is alpha times foreground plus one minus alpha times background. A matting network on a normal image has to guess B too, and its mistakes would become our labels. On a flat screen B is known at every pixel, so that unknown is gone. It's still three equations for four unknowns, so a keyer still guesses. That's why we run three. And pine needles on green? The key eats them. On blue, much better.

slides.title: Pick the screen
slides.speech: So we pick the screen color per prompt. Generate the plain prompt once with SDXL, take a hue histogram weighted by saturation, and choose the named color the object uses least. She's all reds and some blues, so she gets green. Over 90 percent of the dataset ends up green or blue.

slides.title: Keyable images
slides.speech: Catch is, SDXL, Midjourney and DALL-E make dark gradient screens or tint the subject green. DeepFloyd, left, gives a flat screen, but mushy hair. So we chain them. Cut DeepFloyd's girl out roughly with Photoshop, paste her on brighter green, and run SDEdit, SDXL image-to-image, at strength 0.95. That repaints almost everything, Photoshop's rough cut included, so DeepFloyd only donates the layout and a clean screen. Green goes in the negative prompt: it strips spill off the girl, but the screen is too saturated to suppress.

slides.title: Three keyers

elements.text: Agreement is our proxy for correctness.
Score: worst-pair MS-SSIM · above median 0.984: auto, 110k · human picks 1 of 7: 40k

slides.speech: Three keyers that fail differently: a per-pixel color-difference keyer, using a background we get by deleting the object and inpainting; Adobe's internal learned chroma keyer; and Photoshop subject select. Top row cutouts, bottom row alphas. The score composites each cutout on white and on black and takes the worst pair's MS-SSIM. Right, 0.995, all agree. Left, a glass of water, they don't. Agreement is a proxy, not proof: generated images have no ground truth, but keyers that work differently rarely agree on the same wrong answer. Above the median, 0.984, we auto-accept with the open pixel-wise keyer: 110,000. For 40,000 more, mostly glass and smoke, a human picked one of seven.

slides.title: 150,000 cutouts

elements.text: Matting error on DIM test (SAD, lower is better): either dataset alone 36 / 65 → mix 33
Limits: synthetic (artifacts, domain gap) · uses Photoshop, an internal Adobe keyer, Adobe captions · auto path favors opaque objects

slides.speech: That's MAGICK: 150,000 objects, each with foreground colors, an alpha matte and a caption. Does it help real matting? We trained a matting network on DIM, on MAGICK, and on mixes, and tested on real DIM images. Either dataset alone scores 36 or 65; the best mix gets 33. Mixing beats either alone. Thousands of downloads a month. Limits: it's synthetic, so a stop sign gets a perfect matte and misspelled text. The pipeline leans on Photoshop, Adobe's keyer and Adobe captions, though the auto samples use the open keyer. Auto-accept favors opaque things; transparency was human-picked. Cost: 30,000 dollars of annotation plus 32 A100s for three weeks.

slides.title: Alpha in, image out

elements.text: 52 raters, 27 unseen masks: ours 82% vs Canny 16%, 77% vs sketch 23%

slides.speech: With that data we fine-tuned an SD1.5 ControlNet: give it an alpha matte plus a prompt, and it paints a matching image. No prior model takes alpha, so we compared against sketch-edge and Canny-edge ControlNets on the same base. On 27 unseen masks, 52 people picked the better set for looks and prompt fit. The outputs follow the matte's edges, as you can see, but the study measured looks and prompt fit, not edge accuracy; that metric is future work. So now we control what's in a frame. Nothing yet controls how it moves over time. That's the next handle.
